sentences.simple: If there is anyone who can stand in front of Aslan without their knees knocking, they are either braver than most or else just silly.
sentences.grammar: ‘their’ is used for one person (‘anyone’); ‘either … or else’ gives two choices; ‘knees knocking’ means knees shaking with fear.

sentences.context: He would never have found his way if the moon hadn’t come out
sentences.simple: He would never have found his way if the moon had not come out by the time he got to the other river. (You remember that, when they first arrived at the Beavers’, he had seen a smaller river flowing into the great one lower down.)
sentences.grammar: ‘would never have found … if … had not come out’ talks about the past: the moon did come out, so he did find his way.

sentences.context: he might have given up the whole plan and gone back and owned up
sentences.simple: In fact I really think he might have given up the whole plan, gone back, told the truth and made friends with the others, if he had not happened to say to himself, “When I’m King of Narnia the first thing I shall do will be to make some decent roads.”
sentences.grammar: ‘might have + given up’ tells what was possible in the past but did not happen; ‘if he hadn’t happened to say’ gives the reason it did not; ‘owned up’ means ‘told the truth’.

sentences.context: If you hadn’t all been in such a plaguey fuss when we were starting
sentences.simple: If you had not all been in such a fuss when we were starting, I would have brought some pillows,” said Mrs. Beaver.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + had been … I’d have brought’ talks about an unreal past: they were in a fuss, so she did not bring pillows.

sentences.context: It would have been a dreadful thing for the Beavers and the children if the night had remained fine
sentences.simple: It would have been a terrible thing for the Beavers and the children if the night had stayed fine. The wolves would then have been able to follow their trail, and ten to one would have caught them before they got to the cave.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have been … if + had remained’ talks about something that did not happen; ‘ten to one’ means ‘very likely’.

sentences.context: Unless you have looked at a world of snow as long as Edmund had been looking at it
sentences.simple: If you have not looked at a world of snow for as long as Edmund had been looking at it, you will hardly be able to imagine how good those green patches were after the endless white.
sentences.grammar: ‘Unless you have…’ means ‘if you have not…’; ‘had been looking’ is an action that went on up to an earlier past time; ‘hardly’ means ‘almost not’.

sentences.context: If it had not been so angry that it simply had to howl it would have got him by the throat at once
sentences.simple: If it had not been so angry that it simply had to howl, it would have got Peter by the throat at once.
sentences.grammar: ‘so angry that’ gives a result; ‘if it had not been … it would have got’ talks about an unreal past: it did howl, so it did not catch him.

sentences.context: He knows that unless I have blood as the Law says all Narnia will be overturned
sentences.simple: He knows that unless I have blood, as the Law says, all Narnia will be overturned and will be lost in fire and water.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘as the Law says’ means ‘in the way the Law says’; ‘will be overturned’ is passive.

sentences.context: when a willing victim who had committed no treachery was killed in a traitor’s stead
sentences.simple: She would have known that when a willing victim who had not betrayed anyone was killed in the place of a traitor, the Table would crack and Death itself would start working backward.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have known’ means she did not know; ‘who had not betrayed anyone’ gives extra facts about the victim; ‘in a traitor’s stead’ means ‘in the place of a traitor’.

sentences.context: they might have left the body alone
sentences.simple: Oh, it is too bad. They could have left the body alone.
sentences.grammar: ‘might have + left’ means they could have done it but did not; here Lucy is sad and angry about it.

sentences.context: Once the feet are put right, all the rest of him will follow
sentences.simple: Once the feet are put right, all the rest of him will follow.
sentences.grammar: ‘Once + present’ means ‘as soon as’; ‘are put right’ is passive, so it does not say who does it.

sentences.context: It was the same day and the same hour of the day on which they had all gone into the wardrobe
sentences.simple: It was the same day and the same hour of the day when they had all gone into the wardrobe to hide.
sentences.grammar: ‘on which’ is a longer way to say ‘when’; ‘had gone’ is an earlier time than ‘was’.

sentences.context: I know not how it is, but this lamp on the post worketh upon me strangely
sentences.simple: I do not know how it is, but this lamp on the post has a strange effect on me.
sentences.grammar: Old-style speech: ‘I know not’ means ‘I do not know’, and ‘worketh’ means ‘works’; ‘strangely’ means ‘in a strange way’.

sentences.context: if ye will all have it so, let us go on and take the adventure that shall fall to us
sentences.simple: Then in the name of Aslan, if you will all have it so, let us go on and take the adventure that will come to us.
sentences.grammar: Old-style speech: ‘ye’ means ‘you’; ‘have it so’ means ‘want it that way’; ‘shall fall to us’ means ‘will come to us’.

sentences.context: never since we four were Kings and Queens in Narnia have we set our hands to any high matter
sentences.simple: Since we four were Kings and Queens in Narnia, we have never started any big job, such as battles, quests, great deeds of fighting, acts of justice and the like, and then given it up. Always, what we have taken in hand, we have finished.
sentences.grammar: ‘never’ at the start makes ‘have’ come before ‘we’ (‘have we set’); this is an old way to speak; ‘given over’ means ‘given up’.

clear up.meaning: Of the weather: to become fine after rain.
clear up.example: Ten to one it’ll clear up in an hour or so.

hand over.meaning: To give a person or thing to someone else.
hand over.example: catch them and hand them over to her

give up.meaning: To hand a person over to someone. Also, with ‘themselves’: to stop fighting and let others take you.
give up.example: they either gave themselves up or took to flight

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know before.

turn into.meaning: To change into something else, or to make someone change into something else.
turn into.example: never have turned him into stone

make up.meaning: To think of a story that is not true. Also, with ‘it’: to be friends again with someone after a fight.
make up.example: she’s just making up a story for fun

make up one's mind.example: almost made up his mind to go home

give away.meaning: With ‘yourself’: to show by mistake what you wanted to keep secret.

pull yourself together.meaning: To control your feelings and be quiet and sensible again.
pull yourself together.example: Susan pulled herself together and said

make out.meaning: To say that something is true when it is not. Also: to see or understand something that is hard to see.
make out.example: you made out she was telling lies

pay out.meaning: To do something bad to a person because they did something bad to you.
pay out.example: to pay Peter out for calling him a beast

set off.meaning: To start going somewhere, or to start to do something.
set off.example: they set off, all carrying their loads

set out.example: we’d set out on a journey with nothing to eat

keep up.meaning: To go as fast as others, so that you are not left behind.

on the move.meaning: Moving from one place to another.

lose one's head.meaning: To stop thinking in a clear way, for example from fear.
lose one's head.example: one of the young squirrels lost its head completely

give the cold shoulder.meaning: To treat someone in a cold, unfriendly way and not pay attention to them.
give the cold shoulder.example: trying to give him the cold shoulder

take no notice.meaning: To pay no attention to something.
take no notice.example: she took no notice of that

come to life.meaning: To start to live and move.
come to life.example: Everywhere the statues were coming to life.

fall back.meaning: To move back, away from the front or from an enemy.

cut off.meaning: To take away by cutting. Also: to stop someone from reaching a place or other people.
cut off.example: we shall be cut off from Aslan

look out.meaning: To be careful and watch for something near.

keep on.meaning: To go on doing something without stopping.
keep on.example: He kept on slipping in the slush

all the same.meaning: Used to say that something is still true after what was just said.
all the same.example: All the same I think he ought to know

no good.meaning: Of no use; it will not help.
no good.example: It was no good trying to run away

by the way.meaning: Used to add something that you have just thought of.
by the way.example: And, by the way,” said the Queen

look alive.meaning: Used to tell people to be quick and pay attention.

stick to.meaning: To keep to something and not change it.

go on.example: Don’t go on talking like that.

for the sake of.meaning: For the purpose of; in order to get or do something.
for the sake of.example: chiefly for the sake of changing the subject
